summary: Specifies encapsulating packets in GRE and UDP headers, so the UDP source port acts as entropy for ECMP load balancing in transit networks.

eli5.summary: Wrapping a package with a label that helps roads share the traffic evenly.

subtitle: Wrapping GRE tunnel traffic in UDP so routers can spread it across multiple paths using the UDP source port.

tldr.problem: Routers that balance load across equal-cost paths hash only the IP addresses and protocol for GRE traffic, so all of a tunnel's packets take one path.
tldr.mechanism: GRE-in-UDP puts a UDP header in front of the GRE header and uses the UDP source port as an entropy value, so existing ECMP hashing can spread flows across paths. Different requirements apply for the general Internet and for a traffic-managed controlled environment.
tldr.outcome: No change is needed in transit routers, and GRE can cross networks that block it natively. The tunnel has no congestion control of its own, so it needs congestion-controlled traffic or a managed network.

sections.title: Why Put GRE Inside UDP
sections.content:
This RFC specifies a generic way to tunnel network protocol packets across an IP network using Generic Routing Encapsulation (GRE, RFC 2784) carried in User Datagram Protocol (RFC 768) headers. The GRE header names the payload type with an EtherType, and the UDP source port can carry extra entropy.

The main motivation is load balancing. Equal-Cost Multipath (ECMP) mechanisms commonly hash the five-tuple: source and destination IP address, source and destination port, and protocol number. For plain GRE only the two addresses and the protocol field take part, so all GRE traffic between two addresses uses a single path. With UDP, the source port adds entropy to the hash.

A second benefit is that GRE-in-UDP can carry GRE across networks and middleboxes that otherwise do not support it. It can also wrap traffic that is already tunneled. Transit routers need no changes, and it works over IPv4 and IPv6.
sections.eli5: If every truck has the same sticker, the road signs send them all down one road. Putting a changing number on each truck lets the signs send them down different roads.

sections.title: Two Deployment Scenarios and Their Rules
sections.content:
Encapsulated packets are ordinary UDP datagrams, so the tunnel must meet the UDP usage requirements of RFC 8085. The tunnel adds no congestion control beyond that of the carried traffic, so it MUST be used only with congestion-controlled traffic (for example IP unicast) and/or within a network managed to avoid congestion.

The RFC therefore defines two cases. A default GRE-in-UDP tunnel suits the general Internet. A TMCE tunnel is for a traffic-managed controlled environment, an IP network that is traffic-engineered or otherwise managed, for example with rate limiters, to avoid congestion. The tunnel cannot detect where it is deployed, so the operator is responsible for meeting the right set of requirements.

Both cases share these rules. The UDP source port used for flow entropy SHOULD come from the ephemeral range 49152-65535. Its use MUST be configurable, so that a single value can be set for all traffic, in which case a random ephemeral port SHOULD be picked. For IPv6 the entropy SHOULD also go in the flow label. Fragmentation SHOULD happen before encapsulation, with the UDP checksum applied to all fragments.

They differ on three points: the UDP checksum (below), and the carried traffic. A default tunnel MUST NOT carry traffic that is not congestion controlled, while a TMCE tunnel MAY, for example MPLS pseudowires or VPNs with provisioned bandwidth. Such a tunnel MUST stay entirely inside the managed network, and measures SHOULD stop the traffic escaping to the Internet, such as packet filters blocking the assigned UDP ports.
sections.eli5: On a public road you must follow all the traffic rules. On a private track owned by one company, where they control how many cars drive on it, some rules can be relaxed, but the cars must not leak onto the public road.

sections.title: The Encapsulation Format
sections.content:
A packet carries an outer IP header, then a UDP header, then a GRE header, then the encapsulated packet. The UDP and GRE headers MUST be applied and removed as a pair at the tunnel ingress and egress.

In the UDP header the source port holds a 16-bit entropy value generated by the encapsulator to identify the inner flow. It SHOULD be in the ephemeral range 49152 to 65535, where the top two bits are set, which leaves fourteen bits of entropy. If entropy cannot be derived or must be disabled, the encapsulator SHOULD use the same source port for all packets of a flow, to avoid reordering. The port for a flow MAY change over time, but an encapsulator SHOULD NOT change it more than once every thirty seconds.

The destination port is 4754 (GRE-in-UDP) or 4755 (GRE-UDP-DTLS), both allocated by IANA. The UDP length covers the eight-byte UDP header, the GRE header and the payload.

In the GRE header the encapsulator sets the Protocol Type field to the EtherType of the packet inside. It MAY set the Key, Sequence Number and Checksum bits and fields as defined in RFC 2784 and RFC 2890. Because the UDP checksum covers the GRE header and payload, it SHOULD be used in preference to the GRE checksum. The GRE Key MAY be used to authenticate the encapsulator, and a packet with an invalid key MUST be dropped.
sections.eli5: The package gets two labels stuck on in a fixed order. One says what is inside. The other has a number that changes from one parcel to the next, to help the sorting machines.

sections.title: Encapsulation Procedures
sections.content:
The encapsulator sets the UDP and GRE headers as described in the format section. Intermediate routers can load-balance the packets with a hash of the UDP five-tuple. The decapsulator removes the UDP and GRE headers and processes the inner packet. GRE keep-alive is not needed to provide entropy, and it is RECOMMENDED not to use it.

On fragmentation, fragments SHOULD be no larger than the path MTU between the tunnel endpoints minus the GRE and UDP overhead, and the same source port SHOULD be used for all fragments so that transit routers send them the same way. If the operator controls the payload MTU, it SHOULD be set to avoid fragmentation.

For quality of service, the encapsulator derives parameters for the outer IP header, such as Diffserv, from the inner packet. Endpoints that support ECN must use the method of RFC 6040 for ECN marking propagation.
sections.eli5: Before wrapping a big parcel, cut it into pieces that fit the delivery truck. Give every piece the same changing number so they all take the same road and arrive together.

sections.title: Securing the Tunnel with DTLS
sections.content:
Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS, RFC 6347) can be used to secure the tunnel. When it is, the UDP destination port MUST be 4755, and that port MUST NOT be used for other traffic. The source port can still carry entropy.

DTLS is limited to a single session for any encapsulator and decapsulator pair, and both IP addresses MUST be unicast, so multicast is not supported with DTLS. A receiver MUST discard any packet that is neither protected by the DTLS session nor part of DTLS negotiation, and SHOULD log the discard. Both tunnel endpoints must be configured to use DTLS.

DTLS SHOULD be used to meet the security requirements of the original traffic. It may be unnecessary if the traffic is already encrypted or the tunnel is inside an operationally secured network.
sections.eli5: DTLS is a locked box for the parcel. Anything that arrives without the lock gets thrown away.

sections.title: UDP Checksum Handling
sections.content:
For IPv4, a non-zero UDP checksum MUST be processed as in RFC 768 and RFC 1122. A decapsulator MUST verify a non-zero checksum before accepting the packet, and by default SHOULD accept packets with a zero checksum. A packet that fails verification MUST be dropped.

For IPv6 the UDP checksum protects both the IPv6 and UDP headers, so a default tunnel MUST use it. A TMCE tunnel MAY be configured with UDP zero-checksum mode, but only if the environment meets at least one condition: packet corruption is known to be exceptionally unlikely, measured corruption is tolerably low, or the carried applications tolerate corrupt or misdelivered packets.

Using zero-checksum mode brings extra requirements. Using the checksum MUST remain the default. The implementation MUST comply with Section 4 and requirement 1 of Section 5 of RFC 6936. The decapsulator SHOULD allow zero checksums on only a single destination port and MUST check that the IPv6 source and destination addresses are valid for the tunnel. The encapsulator SHOULD use different source addresses for each such tunnel. Traffic MUST be actively monitored for errors, and a non-zero checksum that arrives MUST still be verified. The RFC recommends using the GRE checksum when the UDP checksum is not used.
sections.eli5: The checksum is a tiny number that lets the receiver tell if the parcel was squashed on the way. On the private track you may skip it, but only if you are watching for damage.

sections.title: Middleboxes and Backward Compatibility
sections.content:
Many middleboxes read or change UDP port numbers. A NAPT device translates a private address and source port to a public one, and some firewalls assume that bidirectional traffic uses a common pair of ports. A GRE-in-UDP tunnel is unidirectional and varies its source port, which conflicts with both behaviors. If a middlebox is on the path, the tunnel can disable source port entropy, or the middleboxes can be enabled to pass such packets.

IPv6 datagrams with a zero UDP checksum will not pass any middlebox that validates the checksum, such as a firewall. There is no fallback if a path change sends the tunnel through such a device, and the tunnel will be black-holed. With any middlebox on the path, the UDP checksum is RECOMMENDED.

Deployment needs tunnel ingress routers to be upgraded, but no change at transit routers. A decapsulator that does not support GRE-in-UDP does not listen on ports 4754 and 4755, and answers with an ICMP port unreachable message. The sender MUST NOT keep using the encapsulation toward that peer without management intervention.
sections.eli5: Some checkpoints on the road expect every car to come back the way it left. A tunnel that sends one-way traffic with changing numbers can confuse them, so the operator may need to turn the changing number off.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
GRE-in-UDP does not change the security of the payload protocol, and the security considerations of GRE (RFC 2784) apply. DTLS SHOULD be used to secure the tunnel's traffic.

If source port entropy is disabled, a random ephemeral port SHOULD be chosen to reduce exposure to off-path attacks, and it may be changed periodically to help against some DoS attacks. Because a single standardized destination port may increase that exposure, the endpoints may agree on an alternate port, though how they communicate it is out of scope.

A decapsulator is not required to validate the source IP address of tunneled packets, except for IPv6 when zero-checksum mode is used. Skipping validation presupposes effective filtering at the network boundaries. If the GRE Key is used for traffic separation, for example for NVGRE, header corruption is a concern, and at least one of the UDP and GRE checksums MUST be used for both IPv4 and IPv6.
sections.eli5: Pick a random door number so strangers cannot guess it, and lock the parcel if what is inside is secret.
